descripcion_es: Experiences and present results; just, already, yet, ever, never.
resumen: The present perfect (have / has + past participle) connects the past with the present: life experiences without saying when, recent actions with a present result, and situations that continue up to now.

items: Experience (in your life, no date): I've been to Japan twice.
Recent action with a result now: I've lost my keys (and I don't have them).
Situation that started in the past and continues: We've lived here for ten years / since 2016.

filas: at no time (the sentence is affirmative in form) (es: nunca)
a very short time ago (between have and the participle) (es: acabar de)
before now, sooner than expected (es: ya)
up to now (questions) / still (negatives), at the end (es: ya / todavía)
Have you finished yet? / Not yet.

explicacion.texto: If you say when it happened (yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago), use the past simple: I saw that film last year. since takes a starting point (since Monday) and for takes a duration (for three days).
Been and gone: She has been to Paris (she went and came back) versus She has gone to Paris (she is there now).

ejemplos.frase: She hasn't replied to my email yet.
ejemplos.traduccion: Todavía no ha contestado a mi correo.

ejemplos.frase: They've known each other for twenty years.
ejemplos.traduccion: Se conocen desde hace veinte años.

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With since/for, for something that continues, use the present perfect, not the present.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I have visited London last year.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With a finished time in the past, use the past simple.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Have you finished yet the report?
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Have you finished the report yet?
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Yet goes at the end of the sentence.
There is no double negative in English.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the present perfect.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the third use on the card: a situation that started in the past and continues now goes in the present perfect. The clue is since 2019, which marks the starting point. The subject she needs has, and the past participle of live is lived. That is why the answer is has lived ('s lived). In Spanish we say “vive desde”, in the present, but English does not allow She lives here since 2019.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Situation that continues, with since: has + past participle.

errores_previstos.explicacion: A literal copy of the Spanish present: with since for a situation that continues, you need has lived.
With she, third person singular, the auxiliary is has.
The past simple presents something finished; here the situation continues: has lived.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the present perfect.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the experience use on the card: something that has (or hasn't) happened in your life, without saying when. The table shows that never goes between have and the past participle. The subject I needs have, and ride is irregular: ride, rode, ridden. So the answer is have never ridden or 've never ridden. Be careful not to use rode, which is the past simple, not the past participle.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Experience: have never + past participle (ride → ridden).

errores_previstos.explicacion: Rode is the past simple; the present perfect needs the past participle ridden.
In a neutral sentence never goes between have and the past participle: have never ridden.
After have comes the past participle, not the base form: ridden.

ejercicios.frase: We have worked together ___ six months.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that for goes with a duration (how long) and since with a starting point (since when). Six months is a duration, so it takes for. If we said since, we would need a date or a moment: since March. The sentence as a whole is a present perfect of a situation that continues.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Since needs a starting point (since March); six months is a duration and needs for.
During says when something happens within a period, not how long it has lasted until now; here it is for.
A literal copy of Spanish “desde hace”: in English, duration up to now is expressed with for.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with just, already or yet.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's table shows that yet means “up to now” in questions and “still” in negatives, and it goes at the end of the sentence. That is why yet is the normal choice here. The card also accepts already: in a question it expresses surprise because something seems to have been done sooner than expected (“have you booked it already?”). Just does not fit, because it would mean “a moment ago”, and in questions it usually goes between have and the past participle.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In questions, at the end of the sentence, the normal choice is yet; already is also possible if you are surprised that it is already done.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Just means “a very short time ago” and goes between have and the past participle; it does not fit at the end of this question.
Still is not used like this at the end of a present perfect question; here it is yet.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the present perfect.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the second use on the card: a recent action whose result is noticeable now (the bike is not there). The clue is the reaction Oh no!, which shows that what matters is the present consequence, not when it happened. Someone is singular and needs has; take is irregular: take, took, taken. The answer is has taken or 's taken.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Recent action with a present result: has + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¡Oh, no! Alguien se ha llevado mi bici.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Took is the past simple; the past participle of take is taken.
Someone is third person singular: has taken.
With no specific time and a present result, the natural form in British English is has taken (in American English you hear took, but the card asks for the present perfect).

ejercicios.explicacion: The card is clear: if you say when it happened with an expression of finished time (yesterday, last week, ago), you use the past simple. Yesterday is that clue, so the answer is saw, the past of see. In peninsular Spanish you sometimes hear “lo he visto ayer”, but in English I have seen him yesterday is always wrong.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Yesterday indicates finished time: past simple.

por_opcion.have seen: Incorrect: the present perfect cannot be used with a finished time such as yesterday.
por_opcion.saw: Correct: past simple of see, required with yesterday.
por_opcion.see: It is present; it does not match an action from yesterday.

ejercicios.explicacion: This is the experience use on the card, with ever (“at any time”) in the question. The clue is the past participle been, which can only go with have/has. The question is formed with Have + subject + past participle: Have you ever been…?. Been to means “to have visited (a place) and come back”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Experience with ever: Have + subject + past participle.

por_opcion.Did: Did forms past simple questions and is followed by the base form (Did you go?), never by a past participle such as been.
por_opcion.Have: Correct: Have + you + ever + been forms the experience question in the present perfect.
por_opcion.Are: Are does not form tenses with the past participle been in questions of this kind; Are you ever been is ungrammatical.

ejercicios.frase: Mark isn't here. He has ___ to the bank.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card distinguishes between been and gone: has been to = went and has come back; has gone to = has left and is still there. The clue is Mark isn't here: if he is not here, he is still at the bank, so it is gone. Went does not work because it is the past simple, and after has you need the past participle.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Has left and is still there: gone.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mark no está aquí. Ha ido al banco.

por_opcion.been: Has been to the bank would mean that he went and has already come back; it does not fit with Mark not being here.
por_opcion.gone: Correct: has gone to means that he has left and is still there.
por_opcion.went: Went is the past simple; after has you need a past participle.

ejercicios.frase: I've known Lucía ___ we were at school.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the card's rule on since and for: since goes with a starting point and for with a duration. Here the starting point is a clause, we were at school, which marks when the relationship began. That is why it is since. Ago cannot be used with the present perfect, and it also goes after an amount of time (ten years ago).
ejercicios.traduccion: Conozco a Lucía desde que íbamos al colegio.

por_opcion.for: For goes with durations (for ten years), not with a starting point such as we were at school.
por_opcion.since: Correct: since introduces the starting point of a situation that continues.
por_opcion.ago: Ago goes after a period (two years ago) and needs the past simple, not the present perfect.

ejercicios.enunciado: Turn the sentence into a question.
ejercicios.explicacion: According to the card's table, a present perfect question is formed with Have/Has + subject + past participle. You just invert have and they; the past participle finished does not change. Do is not added, because the present perfect already has its own auxiliary (have). Result: Have they finished the project?.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Do they have finished the project?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Do is not used: the auxiliary have moves in front of the subject.
The inversion is missing: Have they finished…?
After have comes the past participle finished, not the base form.

ejercicios.explicacion: This is the classic mistake the card points out: for a situation that started in the past and continues, with since, English uses the present perfect, not the present. In Spanish we say “la conozco desde 2010”, but in English it is I have known her since 2010 (or I've known). Know is a state verb, so it goes in the present perfect simple, not the continuous.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Situation that continues, with since: present perfect.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: with since for something that continues you need have known.
After have comes the past participle known, not the base form.
The past simple presents the relationship as finished; here it continues: have known.

ejercicios.frase: Have you went to the new museum?
respuestas: Have you been to the new museum?
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's rule says that the present perfect is formed with have + past participle, not with the past simple. Went is the past of go; its past participle is gone, but for the experience of having visited a place you use been (went and came back). The answer is Have you been to the new museum?
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: You need the past participle been (visited and came back), not the past form went.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Have you went to the new museum?
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: went is the past simple and cannot go after have.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Have you go to the new museum?
errores_previstos.explicacion: After have comes the past participle (been or gone), not the base form.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Did you went to the new museum?
errores_previstos.explicacion: After did comes the base form (go), and for an experience with no date the natural form is have been.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Have you gone to the new museum?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Have gone means that someone has left and is still there; asked to the person in front of you, it makes no sense. For the experience of visiting a place, use been.

ejercicios.frase: She has bought a car two weeks ago.
respuestas: She bought a car two weeks ago.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card states that with expressions of finished time, and ago is one of them, you use the past simple. Two weeks ago fixes a specific moment in the past, so you must remove has and use the past of buy: bought. The past participle and the past form are the same (bought), but without has the form becomes the past simple.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With ago, use the past simple.
ejercicios.traduccion: Ella se compró un coche hace dos semanas.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She has bought a car two weeks ago.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: ago needs the past simple.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She buyed a car two weeks ago.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Buy is irregular: its past form is bought.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She has bought a car since two weeks.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Since needs a starting point, and buying is a one-off action; with ago, use bought.

respuestas: I have never been to Japan
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the experience use, and the card's table shows that never goes between have and the past participle. The order is: subject (I) + have + never + been + to Japan. Been to is the way of saying that you have visited a place. A literal copy of Spanish “nunca he estado” would put never at the beginning, which in English is only done with emphatic inversion.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Never goes between have and the past participle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Never I have been to Japan
errores_previstos.explicacion: A literal copy of Spanish “Nunca he estado”: never goes between have and the past participle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I have been never to Japan
errores_previstos.explicacion: Never does not go after the past participle, but before it: have never been.

ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that just means “a very short time ago” and goes between has and the past participle. The subject is the film, third person, so it takes has: The film has just started. As the words have no punctuation, the question with inversion, Has the film just started, is also valid. In no case does just go at the end or at the beginning.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Just goes between has and the past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: La película acaba de empezar. (También: ¿Acaba de empezar la película?)

errores_previstos.explicacion: Just goes between has and the past participle: has just started.
Just does not go at the end; its place is between has and started.

descripcion_larga_es: The present perfect (have/has + past participle) links the past with the present: experiences without a date, recent actions with a present effect, and situations that continue up to now. It looks like the Spanish “pretérito perfecto”, but they do not match: with a finished time (yesterday, ago) English requires the past simple, and for Spanish “llevo diez años aquí” it uses the present perfect, not the present. This is where almost all Spanish speakers go wrong.

contexto.que_es: It is a compound tense made up of have or has and the past participle of the verb: She has finished, I've seen it. It presents a past event from the point of view of the present, without placing it at a finished moment.
contexto.por_que_importa: It is one of the most frequently used tenses for talking about experience, recent news and duration, for example when introducing yourself in an interview (I've worked in trade policy for five years). Confusing it with the past simple or the present produces very noticeable mistakes: I know her since 2010 or I have seen him yesterday clearly sound foreign. In exams it is a classic point of assessment.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: It is triggered by ever, never, just, already, yet, since and for, and by questions such as How long…?. It is avoided with expressions of finished time (yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago), which need the past simple. Spanish speakers tend to use the present for what continues (Spanish “vivo aquí desde 2016” → I live here since 2016) and the present perfect with dates, copying the peninsular Spanish “he visto”.
